_doc: Segmentation & device-class policy for netmon. zones: CIDR per network zone. device_classes: MAC (or IP) -> class (iot, camera, media, game, personal, work, server, k8s, infra). allow: internal flows that are OK (src/dst = IP, zone or class, '*' = any; ports = list of numbers or 'port/proto'). Everything else on a sensitive port, from the DMZ, or from IoT/cameras to servers/k8s/ai is a violation. Edit freely.
_doc_device_classes: What kind of device each one is: MAC address (preferred, survives DHCP changes) or IP -> class. Classes: iot, camera, media, game, personal, work, server, k8s, infra. The class sets a device's risk impact (infra/server 5, k8s/work 4, personal 3, camera/media/game/iot 2) and drives rules: iot and camera devices must not reach protected zones or use admin ports. A device with no class is 'unclassified' and takes its zone's impact. 'Discover from UniFi' guesses classes from UniFi fingerprints; review them.
_doc_zone_roles: What each zone is for, which drives the rules: dmz = internet-exposed (any flow from it into another zone is a high-severity violation; risk x1.3), protected = servers/clusters/AI (IoT or camera access and unexpected cross-zone access are flagged; impact 5; risk x1.15), mgmt = IPMI / infrastructure (impact 4), user = PCs and phones (impact 3), iot = IoT, cameras, guests (impact 2, and not allowed to reach protected zones). Zone names are free-form; the role is what counts.
_doc_scan_thresholds: Flags an internal device as a scanner. Within the time range being analysed (24 h for the nightly analysis), netmon counts each internal source's FAILED connections to other internal hosts (Zeek states S0 = no reply, REJ = refused, RSTOS0, SH, OTH). A source is reported as scanning when EITHER number is reached: hosts = distinct destination IPs it failed to reach (a sweep across many machines), or ports = distinct destination ports it failed on (a port scan of few machines). Defaults hosts 20, ports 40. Lower = more sensitive and more false positives (discovery apps such as Sonos/Cast/printers probe many hosts); raise it if known devices keep appearing. Gateway addresses ending in .1 are ignored. Successful connections do not count. Findings show under Posture > Scans and Network > Lateral movement.
_doc_zones: Your network segments: zone name -> subnet (CIDR). Every internal IP is placed in the most specific matching zone; traffic between zones is what segmentation checks, the zone matrix and the lateral-movement graph are built on. An internal IP in no zone is 'internal-other'. 'Discover from UniFi' fills this from your UniFi networks.
_doc_sensitive_ports: Admin / remote-control / lateral-movement ports (SSH 22, SMB 445, RDP 3389, databases, Docker and Kubernetes APIs...). A successful internal connection to one of these that is not covered by an allow rule is a segmentation violation, and its severity is HIGH. Add a port here to treat it as administrative; netmon also has a built-in list of admin ports that is always included.
_doc_discovery_ports: Ports used by normal network discovery and housekeeping (DNS 53, DHCP 67/68, NTP 123, NetBIOS 137/138, mDNS 5353, SSDP 1900, UPnP...). Connections on these are treated as ordinary (LOW severity) and traffic from a device to its gateway (.1) on them is ignored. Add noisy discovery protocols to cut false positives.
_doc_gateway_ports: Ports clients are expected to use towards the gateway (the .1 address of a subnet): DNS, DHCP, NTP, the web UI, Tailscale/STUN. Flows to a gateway on these ports are skipped by the segmentation check. Remove a port to start checking it.
_doc_allow: Expected internal flows that are NOT violations, checked top to bottom. Each rule has src and dst (an IP, a zone name, a device class, or * for any), optional ports (numbers or 'port/proto' such as 41641/udp; empty = any port) and a 'why'. Anything on a sensitive port, from a dmz zone, from IoT/camera to a protected zone, or across zones into a protected zone that no rule allows is reported. Add a rule when a flagged flow is legitimate; keep rules narrow (specific host and ports).
_doc_upload_spike: How sensitive the 'upload-spike' finding is (a device sent unusually much data out; possible exfiltration or a backup). A device is flagged when the data it sent in the analysed range is ALL of: at least min_mb megabytes (default 25; raise it to ignore small uploads), more than times_normal x its own normal (median of its history, default 3), and more than its normal plus mad_factor x its typical day-to-day variation (default 6; this keeps devices with naturally uneven uploads quiet). min_days = days of history needed before judging a device (default 3). severity = high, medium, low, or off to disable the finding. More sensitive: lower min_mb, times_normal and mad_factor. Less sensitive: raise them. Applies at the next analysis run. Hosts that legitimately back up to the cloud are better handled by raising min_mb than by turning it off.
_doc_beacon: How strict beacon (C2-style periodic connection) detection is. For each internal-to-internet pair (source, destination, port) netmon scores how regular the timing and sizes of its connections are (0 = random, 1 = clockwork) and how many hours of the range it covers. A pair is reported when it has at least min_conns connections, at least min_intervals gaps between them, a score of at least min_score, and activity in at least min_coverage of the hours (0.4 = 40 %). Lower min_score / min_coverage / min_conns = more sensitive (catches slower or sloppier beacons, more false positives from update checks and chat apps); raise them to see only strong, steady beacons. unlabelled_min_score = score at which a beacon to a bare IP (no DNS name or SNI) is reported even in the first days before a baseline exists. ignore_ports = destination ports never examined (default 3478 and 19302, STUN/WebRTC, which are periodic by design). Domains in Known benign > beacon_domains and NTP (123) are excluded afterwards. Applies at the next analysis run.
_doc_spike_thresholds: Sensitivity of the 'jump above normal' findings, one row each: dns_long_names (queries with names of 60+ characters), dns_volume (DNS queries per device), signature_spike (IDS rule hit counts), fan_out (distinct internet hosts contacted) and failed_conns (rejected / unanswered connections). Columns: min = absolute floor (the value must reach it); times_normal = it must also exceed this multiple of the device's own normal; mad_factor = and exceed normal plus this many times its usual day-to-day variation; min_days = days of history required; severity = high, medium, low or off. Lower the numbers for more findings, raise them for fewer. Applies at the next analysis run.
